analysis.one_liner: Phases out feeding medically important antibiotics to healthy farm animals to slow drug resistance.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond being sent to a House subcommittee, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drugmakers to prove that antibiotics routinely fed to healthy cattle, pigs, and poultry pose no risk of creating drug-resistant bacteria, and would have withdrawn approval for nontherapeutic uses — growth promotion and routine disease prevention in crowded conditions — within two years unless that proof was made. It also required manufacturers to report and publish annual sales of these drugs by animal type. Roughly 70 percent of antibiotics sold in the United States go to farm animals without a prescription, and the bill's own findings cite federal and National Academy of Sciences reports linking that practice to the decline of antibiotics that work against human infections.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics to treat common infections like Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli illnesses. The bill's findings cite a National Academy of Sciences estimate that drug-resistant bacteria already cost Americans $4-5 billion per year, and that phasing out feed additives would cost each consumer less than $5-10 annually. It would also have given the public annual data on how much of these drugs are sold and for what purpose, which is not disclosed today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who may ever need an antibiotic

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws approval for nontherapeutic feeding of medically important antibiotics to food animals two years after enactment unless manufacturers can show a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance, preserving the effectiveness of drugs people depend on for infections.

The bill's findings cite a federal interagency task force calling antibiotic resistance 'a growing menace to all people,' a 2003 National Academy of Sciences report concluding that cutting human antibiotic use alone will have little effect without reducing agricultural overuse, and a GAO study linking resistant Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli to antibiotic use in animals.

Requires manufacturers to report annual sales of these drugs by animal type and purpose, and directs the government to publish that data, giving the public information that is currently treated as confidential business information.
The findings note that the European Union banned such feeding in 1999 and saw resistant bacteria levels decline sharply with no significant impact on animal health, food safety, or meat prices.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that sell antibiotics for routine feed use, and livestock operations that rely on growth promotion and routine medication to compensate for crowded, unsanitary conditions. Consumers might pay somewhat more for meat in the short run, though the bill cites a National Academy of Sciences estimate of under $5-10 per person per year and the EU experience of no significant price impact.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal-drug makers and large livestock operations

drawbacks.text: Farmers and drugmakers argue the causal link between agricultural antibiotic use and human resistance is contested, and the bill would force the withdrawal of long-approved products unless manufacturers can meet a high proof standard within two years — a fast timeline for new safety studies.

The bill itself acknowledges certain non-routine uses are legitimate for preventing animal disease, so some disease-prevention uses would continue and the line between 'routine' and justified prevention could require difficult case-by-case determinations.

Supporters' own estimate that meat prices would barely move rests on the European experience, which involved different farming systems; American producers could face real transition costs, and the NAS figure of $5-10 per consumer covers feed additives only, not all the affected uses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are long-term but large: antibiotics that stop working are costly and, in some cases, impossible to replace, and the bill's findings point to a scientific consensus that agricultural overuse is a major contributor. The costs fall on a narrow set of producers and drugmakers, with an estimated consumer cost of a few dollars a year. The main honest objection is the two-year deadline and the burden it places on farmers mid-transition, though the EU precedent cited in the bill suggests those costs were manageable. On balance the public-health benefit outweighs the concentrated cost, which is presumably why the bill never advanced: the parties who would bear the cost had every incentive to keep it from moving.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to its Health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on May 24, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On June 3, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health — the standard step where bills in this area go to wait — and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never advanced to a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's findings cite support from more than 300 health, consumer, agricultural, environmental, and humane organizations, including the American Medical Association and the American Public Health Association.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The animal-health pharmaceutical companies that sell antibiotics for routine feed use and the livestock operations that rely on them are better off, since the status quo — nontherapeutic antibiotic feeding without new safety proof or public sales data — continued unchanged. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria continued to develop at the rate the bill's findings described.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal-drug makers and large livestock producers

for.name: Rep. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out nontherapeutic antibiotic use in food animals and referred it to committee.

for.name: 15 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

for.name: More than 300 health, consumer, agricultural, environmental, and humane organizations
for.role: Supporting coalition cited in the bill's findings, including the American Medical Association and American Public Health Association
for.what_they_did: Supported phasing out nontherapeutic antibiotic use in farm animals, as catalogued in the bill's own findings section.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never held a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Animal-health drugmakers and livestock industry interests
against.role: Industries whose products and practices the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: No industry support appears in the record; the bill, which would have withdrawn approvals for a major segment of their business, received no hearing or vote in a committee with jurisdiction over it.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee run by a Republican chairman with no hearing, vote, or floor action of any kind.

industries.note: Antibiotics sold for routine feed use make up the large majority of U.S. antibiotic sales by volume, per the bill's finding that about 70 percent go to farm animals without a prescription. The bill would withdraw approval for those uses unless the manufacturer proves they are safe, directly cutting a major market.

These operations use nonprescription antibiotics for growth promotion and to offset crowded, unsanitary conditions. The bill would end routine feeding of medically important drugs, requiring management changes; supporters' evidence suggests the cost to consumers would be a few dollars a year, and the EU saw no hit to productivity.
